title: The noble search
hookLine: the ignoble search chases what ages; the noble search seeks the unaging
carry: worth a search of its own

lines: A SEARCH HISTORY IS A DIARY.
cards: Scroll back through a phone's search history. Shoes. Flights.
A better job. Is this mole normal. Houses we can't afford.
Whether a certain person is still single. It's a strange and honest diary of what we're hunting for, day after day. In MN 26 the Buddha says there are two kinds of search.
And he admits, plainly, which kind he once made himself, before his awakening.

teach.b: The Ariyapariyesana Sutta is the twenty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. Ariya means noble; pariyesana means search.
In the ignoble search, a person who is themselves subject to aging, sickness and death looks for happiness in things that are also subject to aging, sickness and death.
He lists them plainly: wife and children, men and women slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, horses, gold and silver. None of these is wicked.

teach.h: CHASING WHAT AGES, AS YOU AGE
teach.b: The point is only that they age too: you're chasing something that is running out at the same speed you are.
In the noble search, a person who sees that they are subject to aging and death looks for what does not age and does not die: the unborn, the deathless, the supreme security from bondage.
Buddhists call it nibbana, nirvana in Sanskrit. Then the Buddha tells his own story, in his own voice.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA'S OWN SEARCH, TOLD BY HIM
teach.b: Before awakening, he too was making the ignoble search. Then, while still young, black-haired, in the first stage of life, he shaved his head and went forth, though his mother and father wept.
He studied with two teachers, Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, mastered what they taught, and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search.
He walked until he reached a pleasant grove at Uruvela with a clear river, sat down, and there found what he was looking for.
So the noble search isn't throwing away the shoes or the house. It's noticing what you're asking them to do. They can't stop you aging.
Something else might be worth a search of its own.

how: MN 26 is read as the Buddha's own account of his going forth and awakening, and teachers use its two searches to invite reflection on aging, sickness and death.

o: a pilgrimage to the holy places of India
a monk's daily round, begging for food
the search for what doesn't age or die

games.q: inside the noble search — tap the pairs.
p: chasing what ages, as you age

s: the Buddha says family and possessions are wicked
they aren't wicked; they simply age and pass, like the one who seeks them.
in MN 26 the Buddha tells his own story
he says he too made the ignoble search, then went forth while young, though his parents wept.
he stayed with his first two teachers to the end
he mastered what they taught and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search.

games.q: you've mastered everything a well-known teacher knows. he offers to share leadership of his community with you. what do you do?
o: leave: this isn't the end of the search.
start a rival community next door.
games.why: in MN 26 the young seeker leaves both of his teachers, because what they taught didn't lead all the way to the deathless.

practice: Think of the last three things you searched for, on a screen or in your head, and hold each one lightly: will this age?
Then ask what in you was looking underneath, rest, safety, to be loved, and let that deeper wish sit with you as you breathe, without solving it.

wordCard.voice: ariyapariyesana. A being who ages, seeking what does not age.

orig.note: Pali pariyesana: search, seeking. ariyapariyesana: the noble search.

carryVoice: Your line: worth a search of its own. Nothing wrong with the shoes; they just can't do that job. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26, Ariyapariyesana Sutta (the noble search)
